passage:
Saturday
We WON the basketball match! I scored the last basket with two seconds left. Everyone screamed. Nandini Ma'am hugged the whole team.
But Rohit went quiet. He sat on the bench, untying and retying his shoes. He'd wanted that last shot. He'd practised all week.
I felt a bit awkward. Then I remembered: he passed me the ball. Without that pass, there was no basket.
So I went over. "Rohit, that pass was perfect. You set it up."
He looked up. "Really?"
"Really. Want to practise free throws together tomorrow?"
He nodded. I'm still really happy I scored. But it was both of us.
Mridul

qa.q: How many seconds were left when Mridul scored?
qa.a: Two seconds.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when Rohit went quiet?
qa.a: Mridul felt awkward, still happy about scoring but uneasy, knowing Rohit had wanted that last shot after practising all week.

qa.q: What did Mridul do that was wise?
qa.a: Mridul credited Rohit's pass and invited him to practise, without pretending the basket didn't matter.

qa.q: How might Rohit feel after Mridul praised the pass?
qa.a: Rohit would likely feel seen and included, and less left out of the win.

grounding: Mridul scores the winning basket and a teammate goes quiet; Mridul credits his pass and includes him without downplaying the win completely.

At the village football match, Asif scored the winning goal in the last minute. The crowd by the banyan tree cheered wildly.
But Kunal, who had been clapping a second ago, suddenly went silent. He walked to the edge of the field and kicked at the grass. Asif knew Kunal had been dreaming of that winning goal all season.
Asif went over. "Kunal, I only scored because of your cross. It was brilliant."
Kunal shrugged. "You still scored."
"Yes, and I'm happy about it. But it was your ball. Next match, you take the penalty if we get one."
Kunal looked up and smiled a little.

qa.q: Where did the crowd cheer?
qa.a: By the banyan tree.

qa.q: How did Asif feel when he saw Kunal kicking at the grass?
qa.a: Asif felt happy about his goal but also sympathetic and a little uneasy, knowing Kunal had dreamed of that goal all season.

qa.q: How did Asif handle Kunal's sulking?
qa.a: He credited Kunal's cross and offered him the next penalty, while still being happy about his own goal.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel after Asif's offer?
qa.a: Kunal seemed to feel better and included, smiling a little.

grounding: A boy scores the winning goal and a teammate sulks; he credits the teammate's cross and includes him, without downplaying himself entirely.

I'm Aditi. Last summer, Salma and I played chess every evening on her balcony. One day she went to answer the door, and I saw it: if I moved her bishop back one square, I'd have checkmate in two.
She would never know. My hand even hovered over the board.
Winning against Salma would feel so big. Losing always made me feel small.
But I imagined winning like that. I'd have to hide it every time she said, "Good game." The win would feel empty.
I pulled my hand back. When Salma returned, we played on. I lost. But I didn't have anything to hide.

qa.q: Where did Aditi and Salma play chess?
qa.a: On Salma's balcony.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when her hand hovered over the board?
qa.a: Aditi felt tempted, because winning would feel big and losing always felt small.

qa.q: Why did Aditi decide to play fair?
qa.a: Aditi realised a win by cheating would feel empty and would need to be hidden every time Salma said "Good game".

qa.q: How might Salma have felt if she found out?
qa.a: Salma would likely feel betrayed and hurt that her friend cheated.

grounding: Aditi could bend a rule unnoticed but realises a cheated win would feel empty and need hiding, and plays fair.

Summer camp leader's note, Thursday.
During carrom this afternoon, Ganga and Jagdish were tied. When Jagdish turned to talk to a friend, the queen slid off the board onto the floor near Ganga's foot.
Ganga could have put it back in the pocket. No one was watching, or so she thought. I saw her pick it up and pause, looking at the pocket.
Then she put it in the centre and said, "Jagdish, the queen fell. It's still in play."
Jagdish won that game. Ganga looked disappointed but calm. When I asked her about it later, she said, "If I won like that, I'd have to keep it secret forever."

passage:
At the Hyderabad inter-school chess tournament, Rafiq touched his knight, then quietly moved his rook instead while Minakshi looked away. It won him the game and the trophy.
Everyone clapped. Minakshi shook his hand. "Well played."
At home, the trophy sat on his shelf. Rafiq couldn't look at it. It felt heavy, like a stone in his stomach.
On Monday he went to the chess coach. "Sir, I broke the touch-move rule in the final. Minakshi should have won."
The coach was quiet. Then he said, "Thank you for telling me. You'll have to return the trophy, and apologise to Minakshi."
Rafiq nodded. For the first time in days, he could breathe.

qa.q: Which rule did Rafiq break?
qa.a: The touch-move rule.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel about the trophy at home?
qa.a: He felt guilty and heavy, unable to look at it, like a stone in his stomach.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do to start clean?
qa.a: He admitted it to the coach, accepted returning the trophy and agreed to apologise to Minakshi.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel when she hears the truth?
qa.a: Minakshi may feel surprised and a little hurt, but she might also respect Rafiq for owning up.

grounding: A boy cheats to win a trophy and feels its weight; he admits it to the coach, accepts the consequence and starts clean.

"Coach Alka, can I talk to you?"
"Of course, Nilesh. What's up?"
"The race last week. The 400 metres."
"You won. Well done."

Coach Alka put down her clipboard. "I see."
"The medal's been in my drawer. I can't even look at it."

"I know. What happens now?"
"You'll give the medal to Harish, who came second. And you'll sit out the next meet. But you told me yourself, and that matters."
Nilesh let out a long breath. "Okay. Thank you."

passage:
Tuesday
In the badminton match today, Kunal kept calling my shots "out" even when they were clearly in. The third time, I saw the shuttle land right on the line.
I was SO angry. My face was hot and my hands were shaking. I wanted to call his shots out too, just to get even.
But then I'd be just as bad.
So I walked to the umpire's chair. "Excuse me, Sir, I think that shot was in. Could you watch the line?"
The umpire started watching our court closely. Kunal stopped calling bad lines.
I lost 21-19. But I didn't cheat back.
Aditi

qa.q: What was Kunal calling Aditi's shots?
qa.a: "Out", even when they were clearly in.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel when Kunal kept calling shots out?
qa.a: Aditi felt furious, face hot and hands shaking, wanting to get even.

qa.q: What did Aditi do instead of cheating back?
qa.a: Aditi calmly asked the umpire to watch the line.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt once the umpire watched closely?
qa.a: Kunal probably felt caught out, since he stopped calling bad lines.

grounding: Aditi catches an opponent cheating and feels furious, but tells the umpire calmly instead of cheating back.

In the village marbles game behind the temple, Afreen saw Asif quietly nudge his marble closer to the line with his toe.
Heat rushed up her neck. She wanted to shout "Cheater!" and scatter his marbles into the dust.
Instead, she took a breath. She walked over to Nizam Chacha, who was sitting on the temple steps and always settled their games.
"Chacha, I think Asif moved his marble with his foot. Can you watch the next round?"
Nizam Chacha came and watched. Asif played the rest fairly, though he glared at her.
Afreen lost the round. But she felt steady. She hadn't turned into a cheater too.

"Tejas, your Chandrika Atya once did a whole group project alone. I was eleven. We had to make a model of the water cycle. Four of us. But the other three just chatted and giggled, every day.
I did everything. Cutting, gluing, painting. And I said nothing. I just got angrier and angrier.
The night before, I was up till midnight, crying over the glue.
My mother said, 'Why didn't you tell them to do their part?' I hadn't thought I could.
Next project, I said on day one: 'Let's split the jobs.' When one girl still didn't help, I told the teacher. It was so much easier."

qa.q: What model did young Chandrika's group have to make?

grounding: An aunt recalls silently doing most of a group project while others chatted; later she asked clearly for tasks to be split and told the teacher.
